title: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand
summary: Bosnian Serb student Gavrilo Princip shoots Austria-Hungary's heir and his wife in Sarajevo, setting off the crisis that leads to World War I.
description: Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife Sophie were shot dead in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, a 19-year-old member of the Young Bosnia movement who had been armed with the help of the Serbian nationalist secret society known as the Black Hand. Austria-Hungary, backed by Germany, issued an ultimatum to Serbia and declared war on 28 July. Within a week the alliance system had drawn in Russia, Germany, France and Britain in what became known as the July Crisis. Historians still debate how far responsibility for the escalation lies with Germany, Austria-Hungary, Russia or the alliance system as a whole.

title: World War I
summary: The Allies and the Central Powers fight a global industrial war that kills around 9 million soldiers and millions of civilians.
description: The war pitted the Allies (chiefly France, the British Empire, Russia, Italy from 1915 and the United States from 1917) against the Central Powers (Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria). After German armies were halted at the First Battle of the Marne in September 1914, the Western Front settled into trench warfare stretching from the Channel to Switzerland, while fighting also raged in Eastern Europe, the Middle East, Africa and at sea. Machine guns, heavy artillery, poison gas, tanks, aircraft and submarines made it the first fully industrialised war. It ended with the collapse of four empires — the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman — and redrew the map of Europe and the Middle East.

title: Gallipoli campaign
summary: An Allied attempt to force the Dardanelles and knock the Ottoman Empire out of the war ends in costly failure and evacuation.
description: British and French warships tried to force the Dardanelles strait in early 1915, and after that failed, British, French, Indian, Australian and New Zealand troops landed on the Gallipoli peninsula on 25 April. Ottoman forces, including a division led by Mustafa Kemal (later Atatürk), confined the invaders to narrow beachheads, and the Allies withdrew by January 1916 after roughly half a million casualties on both sides combined. The landing date is commemorated as Anzac Day in Australia and New Zealand, where the campaign became central to national identity, and Kemal's role helped launch his political career.

title: Armenian genocide
summary: The Ottoman government systematically deports and kills Armenians; an estimated 600,000 to 1.5 million die in massacres and death marches.
description: Beginning with the arrest of Armenian intellectuals and community leaders in Constantinople on 24 April 1915, the Committee of Union and Progress government ordered the deportation of the Armenian population of Anatolia, accusing it of siding with Russia. Men were frequently massacred outright, while women, children and the elderly were driven on death marches into the Syrian Desert, where many perished in camps around Deir ez-Zor, the place marked here. Assyrians and Greeks of the empire suffered parallel atrocities. Most historians and genocide scholars, and many governments, recognise the events as genocide, a classification that the Republic of Turkey continues to reject.

title: Einstein presents general relativity
summary: Albert Einstein presents the field equations of general relativity to the Prussian Academy of Sciences, recasting gravity as curved spacetime.
description: After nearly a decade of work, Einstein delivered the final form of his field equations in Berlin, describing gravity not as a force but as the curvature of spacetime by mass and energy. The theory immediately explained the anomalous advance of Mercury's perihelion, and its predicted bending of starlight was confirmed during the solar eclipse of 29 May 1919 by British expeditions organised by Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson, making Einstein world-famous. General relativity underpins modern cosmology, black-hole physics and the detection of gravitational waves in 2015, and its corrections are essential to satellite navigation systems such as GPS.

title: Battle of Verdun
summary: German and French armies fight for ten months around the fortress city of Verdun, one of the longest and costliest battles in history.
description: The German Chief of Staff Erich von Falkenhayn attacked the fortified region of Verdun hoping, by his own later account, to bleed the French army white. French forces under Philippe Pétain and later Robert Nivelle held the line under the slogan 'They shall not pass', and by December had retaken most of the lost ground, including Fort Douaumont. Casualties totalled roughly 700,000 killed, wounded and missing, divided fairly evenly between the two sides. Verdun became a lasting symbol of French endurance and of the futility of attritional warfare.

title: Battle of the Somme
summary: An Anglo-French offensive on the Somme costs over a million casualties; the British army suffers 57,000 casualties on the first day alone.
description: Intended partly to relieve pressure on the French at Verdun, the offensive opened after a week-long bombardment that failed to cut the German wire or destroy deep dugouts. On 1 July the British army suffered about 57,000 casualties, including more than 19,000 dead, the bloodiest day in its history. Over four and a half months the Allies advanced only about 10 km, at a combined cost on all sides of more than one million casualties. The battle saw the first use of tanks in September 1916, and historians continue to debate whether its attritional effect on the German army justified the losses.

title: October Revolution: the Bolsheviks take power
summary: Lenin's Bolsheviks overthrow Russia's Provisional Government in Petrograd, founding the world's first communist state.
description: The February Revolution of March 1917 had already forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate, ending three centuries of Romanov rule, but the Provisional Government that replaced him kept Russia in the war and lost popular support. On the night of 7–8 November, Bolshevik-led Red Guards seized key points in Petrograd and the Winter Palace, and Vladimir Lenin's Council of People's Commissars took power in the name of the soviets. The new regime made a separate peace with Germany at Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 and won a brutal civil war that lasted until about 1922, the year the Soviet Union was founded. The revolution shaped twentieth-century politics, inspiring communist movements worldwide and defining the ideological divide of the Cold War.

title: Spanish flu pandemic
summary: An H1N1 influenza pandemic infects about a third of the world's people and kills tens of millions, with estimates from 17 to 50 million or more.
description: The pandemic spread in several waves, the deadliest in autumn 1918, carried by troop movements and wartime shipping to almost every inhabited region, including remote Pacific islands and the Arctic. Unusually, it killed many healthy young adults, often through secondary bacterial pneumonia, for which there were then no antibiotics. Its name comes from neutral Spain, whose uncensored press reported on it freely; the true origin is uncertain, with hypotheses including Kansas, where an early outbreak was recorded at Camp Funston in March 1918 (the place marked here), northern France and China. Death toll estimates range from about 17 million to 50 million or more, making it one of the deadliest pandemics in history.

title: Armistice ends the fighting of World War I
summary: Germany signs an armistice in a railway carriage near Compiègne, and the guns fall silent on the Western Front at 11 a.m.
description: With its allies collapsing, its army in retreat and revolution spreading at home, Germany sought terms, and its delegates signed the armistice in Marshal Ferdinand Foch's railway carriage in the Forest of Compiègne at about 5 a.m. Fighting ended six hours later, at 11 a.m. Paris time, although men continued to die in attacks up to the final minutes. Kaiser Wilhelm II's abdication had been announced two days earlier, without his consent, as Germany was proclaimed a republic; he crossed into the Netherlands on 10 November and formally abdicated on 28 November. The date is marked as Armistice Day or Remembrance Day in many countries, and the formal peace terms followed at Versailles in 1919.

title: Treaty of Versailles
summary: The Allies and Germany sign the main peace treaty of World War I in the Hall of Mirrors, imposing territorial losses, disarmament and reparations.
description: Negotiated at the Paris Peace Conference largely by the leaders of Britain, France, the United States and Italy, the treaty was signed exactly five years after the Sarajevo assassination. Germany lost about 13 percent of its European territory and all its colonies, had its army limited to 100,000 men, and accepted responsibility for the war's damage under Article 231, the basis for reparations. The treaty also created the League of Nations. Its harshness was bitterly resented in Germany and has long been debated: some historians, following John Maynard Keynes, saw it as a cause of later instability, while others argue that its terms were less punitive than often claimed and that enforcement, not design, failed.

title: League of Nations founded
summary: The first worldwide intergovernmental organisation devoted to keeping the peace comes into being, with its headquarters in Geneva.
description: The League was established when the Treaty of Versailles came into force, embodying US President Woodrow Wilson's vision of collective security, although the US Senate refused to ratify the treaty and the United States never joined. At its height in the 1930s it had 58 member states and achieved successes in settling minor disputes, resettling refugees and tackling disease, the drug trade and forced labour. It proved powerless against aggression by major powers, including Japan's invasion of Manchuria, Italy's conquest of Ethiopia and Germany's rearmament, and could not prevent World War II. It was formally dissolved in 1946, transferring its assets to the United Nations.

title: Irish Free State established
summary: After the Irish War of Independence and the Anglo-Irish Treaty, 26 Irish counties become a self-governing dominion within the British Commonwealth.
description: After the Easter Rising of 1916 and the guerrilla War of Independence from 1919 to 1921, the Anglo-Irish Treaty signed in December 1921 created the Irish Free State as a dominion, while six northeastern counties remained in the United Kingdom as Northern Ireland. Disagreement over the treaty, particularly the oath of allegiance to the Crown and partition, led to the Irish Civil War of 1922–23 between pro- and anti-treaty nationalists. The Free State gradually loosened its ties to Britain, adopting a new constitution as Éire in 1937 and becoming the Republic of Ireland in 1949.

title: March on Rome brings Mussolini to power
summary: Facing a Fascist march on the capital, King Victor Emmanuel III appoints Benito Mussolini prime minister of Italy.
description: Mussolini's National Fascist Party, whose Blackshirt squads had used violence against socialists and trade unions since 1919, mobilised tens of thousands of supporters to converge on Rome. Rather than declare martial law, King Victor Emmanuel III invited Mussolini to form a government on 29 October, and the marchers entered the city afterwards. Over the following years Mussolini dismantled parliamentary democracy, and by 1926 Italy was a one-party dictatorship. Italian Fascism became a model for authoritarian movements across Europe, including German Nazism.

title: Tomb of Tutankhamun discovered
summary: Howard Carter finds the nearly intact tomb of the boy pharaoh Tutankhamun in Egypt's Valley of the Kings.
description: Working for his patron Lord Carnarvon, the British archaeologist Howard Carter uncovered the first step of the tomb, designated KV62, on 4 November 1922, and the burial chamber was opened in February 1923. Though robbers had entered it in antiquity, it was the best-preserved royal tomb ever found in the Valley of the Kings, holding more than 5,000 objects including the solid gold inner coffin and the famous gold funerary mask. The discovery caused a worldwide sensation and a fashion for all things Egyptian, while Carnarvon's death in 1923 gave rise to the popular but unfounded legend of a 'curse of the pharaohs'.

title: Republic of Turkey proclaimed
summary: Mustafa Kemal proclaims the Republic of Turkey in Ankara, completing the end of the six-century-old Ottoman Empire.
description: Defeated in World War I and facing partition under the Treaty of Sèvres, the Ottoman state was effectively supplanted by a nationalist movement led by Mustafa Kemal, which won the Turkish War of Independence against Greek, Armenian, French and British forces. The sultanate was abolished in November 1922, the Treaty of Lausanne of July 1923 recognised Turkey's borders, and the republic was proclaimed that October with Ankara as capital and Kemal as president. The caliphate was abolished in 1924, and Kemal, later surnamed Atatürk, pushed through sweeping secular and Westernising reforms, including a Latin-based alphabet and new civil code. The empire's former Arab provinces passed to British and French mandates.

title: Alexander Fleming discovers penicillin
summary: Fleming notices that a Penicillium mould kills bacteria on a culture plate in his London laboratory, the discovery behind the first true antibiotic.
description: Returning from holiday to his laboratory at St Mary's Hospital, Paddington, the Scottish bacteriologist Alexander Fleming observed that a mould contaminating a Staphylococcus culture had cleared the bacteria around it, and he published the finding in 1929. He could not purify the active substance, and it was a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, including Norman Heatley, that isolated penicillin and demonstrated its power in 1940–41. Mass production in the United States and Britain made it widely available to Allied forces by D-Day in 1944. Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the 1945 Nobel Prize, and antibiotics went on to transform medicine, though resistant bacteria are now a growing threat.

title: Wall Street Crash and the Great Depression
dateLabel: Black Tuesday, 29 October 1929; depression through the 1930s
summary: The collapse of US stock prices in October 1929 is followed by the worst economic depression of the industrial era, spreading to almost every country.
description: After a speculative boom, the New York Stock Exchange crashed on 24 and 28–29 October 1929, and a wave of bank failures, collapsing demand and falling prices followed. Between 1929 and 1932 world industrial production and trade fell sharply, and US unemployment reached about 25 percent by 1933, with similar hardship in Germany and much of the commodity-exporting world. Economists still debate the relative roles of the crash, the gold standard, monetary contraction by central banks and protectionist tariffs such as Smoot–Hawley. The Depression discredited laissez-faire economics, gave rise to the New Deal and Keynesian ideas, and fuelled the rise of extremist movements, including Nazism in Germany.

title: Holodomor: famine in Soviet Ukraine
summary: A man-made famine caused by Stalin's forced collectivisation and grain requisitions kills an estimated 3.5 to 5 million people in Ukraine.
description: Forced collectivisation of agriculture and impossible grain-procurement quotas devastated Soviet farming in 1932–33, and famine struck Ukraine, Kazakhstan, the North Caucasus and the Volga region. In Ukraine, whose capital was then Kharkiv, the authorities blacklisted villages that failed to meet quotas, confiscated remaining food and, from January 1933, restricted peasants from leaving in search of food. Most estimates put Ukrainian deaths at roughly 3.5 to 5 million, and at least 1.5 million people died in the parallel famine in Kazakhstan. Whether the Ukrainian famine was a deliberate genocide against Ukrainians as a nation is debated by historians; Ukraine and many other states recognise it as genocide, while some scholars see it primarily as the result of brutal policies applied across the Soviet Union.

title: Hitler becomes Chancellor of Germany
summary: President Hindenburg appoints Nazi leader Adolf Hitler chancellor; within months Germany becomes a one-party dictatorship.
description: The Nazi Party had become the largest party in the Reichstag in July 1932 amid mass unemployment, and conservative politicians around Franz von Papen persuaded President Paul von Hindenburg to appoint Hitler at the head of a coalition, believing they could control him. After the Reichstag fire of 27 February 1933, emergency decrees suspended civil liberties, and the Enabling Act of March gave the cabinet power to make laws without parliament. By July all other parties had been banned or dissolved, and after Hindenburg's death in August 1934 Hitler combined the offices of chancellor and president as Führer. The regime soon began persecuting Jews, political opponents and other groups, and rearmed Germany in preparation for war.

title: Stalin's Great Purge
summary: Stalin's secret police arrest some 1.5 million people and execute about 680,000 in 1937–38 alone in a campaign of political terror.
description: Following the murder of Leningrad party chief Sergei Kirov in 1934, Joseph Stalin's regime turned on supposed enemies within the Communist Party, the state, the Red Army and society at large. Show trials in Moscow convicted leading Old Bolsheviks such as Grigory Zinoviev, Lev Kamenev and Nikolai Bukharin on fabricated charges, while the NKVD's mass operations of 1937–38 targeted peasants, ethnic minorities and ordinary citizens under arrest quotas. Official records show about 680,000 executions in those two years, with hundreds of thousands more dying in the Gulag labour camps. The purge of the officer corps weakened the Red Army on the eve of World War II.

title: Spanish Civil War
summary: A military uprising against Spain's Republic leads to a three-year civil war won by General Francisco Franco's Nationalists.
description: A coup by right-wing army officers against the elected Popular Front government split Spain between Republicans, supported by the Soviet Union, Mexico and volunteer International Brigades, and Nationalists, backed by Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany. The war became a testing ground for new weapons and tactics, epitomised by the German bombing of Guernica in April 1937, which Pablo Picasso commemorated in his painting. Estimates of deaths, including executions behind both lines, run from about 300,000 to 500,000. Franco ruled Spain as a dictator until his death in 1975.

title: Second Sino-Japanese War
summary: A clash at the Marco Polo Bridge near Beijing grows into full-scale war between Japan and China that merges into World War II and kills millions of Chinese.
description: Japan had seized Manchuria in 1931 and set up the puppet state of Manchukuo, and a skirmish at the Marco Polo Bridge outside Beiping (Beijing) on 7 July 1937 escalated into all-out war. Japanese forces took Shanghai, the Nationalist capital Nanjing, where they carried out a notorious massacre, and Wuhan, and by the end of 1938 held most of eastern China's coast, major cities and railways, while Chiang Kai-shek's government retreated to Chongqing. The Nationalists and Mao Zedong's Communists formed an uneasy united front, and the war settled into a costly stalemate marked by the bombing of cities, Japanese 'Three Alls' reprisal campaigns and chemical and biological warfare, and the deliberate breaching of the Yellow River dikes by Nationalist forces in 1938. After the attack on Pearl Harbor in December 1941 the conflict merged into World War II, and it ended with Japan's surrender in 1945. Chinese deaths, military and civilian, are commonly estimated at about 14 to 20 million, and the war weakened the Nationalists and helped the Communists win the civil war that followed.

title: Nanjing Massacre
summary: Japanese troops capturing China's capital kill tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands of civilians and prisoners over about six weeks.
description: After the Marco Polo Bridge Incident of July 1937 escalated into full-scale war between Japan and China, Japanese forces captured Nanjing, then the Nationalist capital, on 13 December. Over the following weeks soldiers carried out mass killings of disarmed troops and civilians, widespread rape and looting, while a small group of Westerners organised a safety zone that sheltered many residents. Estimates of the dead vary widely, from about 40,000 to over 300,000; the postwar Tokyo tribunal put the figure above 200,000 and China officially cites 300,000. Denial or minimisation by some Japanese nationalists remains a source of tension between the two countries.

title: World War II
summary: The deadliest conflict in history, fought between the Axis and the Allies across Europe, Asia, Africa and the oceans, kills 70–85 million people.
description: The war in Europe began with Germany's invasion of Poland, while in Asia fighting between Japan and China had been under way since 1937. Germany, Italy, Japan and their allies (the Axis) initially conquered much of Europe, North Africa, East Asia and the Pacific, before the alliance of the British Empire, the Soviet Union, the United States, China and others (the Allies) reversed their gains from 1942–43. Most of the dead were civilians, killed by genocide including the Holocaust, by bombing, massacres, famine and disease. The war ended with Germany's surrender in May 1945 and Japan's in August–September after the atomic bombings. It left the United States and the Soviet Union as rival superpowers, led to the founding of the United Nations, and accelerated decolonisation.

title: Germany invades Poland
summary: German forces attack Poland, prompting Britain and France to declare war; the Soviet Union invades from the east on 17 September.
description: The campaign opened with the shelling of the Polish garrison at Westerplatte near Danzig (Gdańsk) by the battleship Schleswig-Holstein and a massive assault by German armoured and air forces. Britain and France declared war on Germany on 3 September but offered little direct help. Under the secret protocol of the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact signed in August, the Soviet Union invaded eastern Poland on 17 September, and the country was partitioned between the two powers by early October. Both occupiers carried out mass repression, including the Soviet Katyn massacre of Polish officers in 1940 and German persecution that culminated in the Holocaust.

title: Battle of Britain
summary: RAF Fighter Command defeats the German Luftwaffe's attempt to win air superiority over Britain, forcing Hitler to postpone an invasion.
description: After the fall of France in June 1940, Germany sought control of the air over southern England as a precondition for a seaborne invasion, codenamed Operation Sea Lion. The Royal Air Force, aided by a radar-based early-warning and control system and by pilots from across the Commonwealth, Poland and Czechoslovakia, inflicted unsustainable losses on the Luftwaffe. From September Germany shifted to bombing London and other cities in the Blitz, which continued into May 1941. The battle, the first fought mainly in the air, kept Britain in the war as a base for the later liberation of Western Europe.

title: Operation Barbarossa: Germany invades the USSR
summary: Some 3.8 million Axis troops invade the Soviet Union along a front of about 2,900 km, the largest land invasion in history.
description: Breaking the 1939 non-aggression pact, Germany and its allies attacked on a front from the Baltic to the Black Sea, opening the war's largest and deadliest theatre; among the first targets was the border fortress of Brest, marked here. The Soviet defenders were caught largely unprepared, and by autumn the Germans had encircled millions of Red Army soldiers, besieged Leningrad and reached the outskirts of Moscow. The offensive stalled in mud and cold, and a Soviet counteroffensive launched on 5 December pushed the Germans back from the capital. Conceived as a war of annihilation, the invasion was accompanied by mass shootings of Jews by the Einsatzgruppen, and about 2 million Soviet prisoners captured that year had died in German captivity by early 1942, mostly of starvation.

title: The Holocaust
summary: Nazi Germany and its collaborators systematically murder about six million European Jews, along with millions of others they deemed undesirable.
description: Persecution of Jews in Germany began after the Nazis took power in 1933, escalating through the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 and the Kristallnacht pogrom of 1938. After the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, mobile killing units shot well over a million Jews, and the regime moved to the 'Final Solution', coordinated at the Wannsee Conference in January 1942, deporting Jews from across occupied Europe to extermination camps such as Treblinka, Sobibor, Bełżec and Auschwitz-Birkenau; at Auschwitz alone about 1.1 million people were murdered. In total about six million Jews, roughly two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, were killed. The Nazis also murdered Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners of war, Poles and other groups. The Holocaust shaped postwar international law, including the concept of genocide and the Genocide Convention of 1948.

title: Attack on Pearl Harbor
summary: A surprise Japanese carrier air raid on the US Pacific Fleet in Hawaii kills about 2,400 Americans and brings the United States into the war.
description: Seeking to secure the resources of Southeast Asia after a US oil embargo, Japan launched some 350 aircraft from six carriers against the naval base at Pearl Harbor on Oahu, sinking or damaging eight battleships. The US aircraft carriers were at sea and escaped, and the base's fuel depots and repair facilities were largely spared. Within hours Japan also attacked the Philippines, Malaya, Hong Kong, Guam and Wake Island. The United States declared war on Japan the next day, and Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on 11 December, joining the European and Asian wars into a single global conflict.

title: Battle of Stalingrad
summary: The Soviet Red Army destroys the German Sixth Army at Stalingrad on the Volga, a turning point of the war in Europe.
description: The German summer offensive of 1942 aimed at the oil fields of the Caucasus, and the city bearing Stalin's name on the Volga became the scene of months of brutal street fighting. In November 1942 the Soviet counteroffensive, Operation Uranus, broke through the Romanian-held flanks and encircled about 300,000 Axis troops. Field Marshal Friedrich Paulus surrendered with the southern pocket on 31 January 1943, and the last Sixth Army troops in the northern pocket gave up on 2 February; only about 6,000 of the roughly 91,000 prisoners taken eventually returned home. With combined military and civilian casualties often estimated at close to 2 million, it was among the bloodiest battles in history.

title: Bengal famine of 1943
summary: Famine in wartime British-ruled Bengal kills an estimated 2 to 3 million people, as food prices soar and relief comes late.
description: In 1942–43 Bengal suffered a series of shocks: the Japanese conquest of Burma cut off rice imports, a cyclone in October 1942 and a fungal disease damaged the rice crop, and wartime military spending drove rapid inflation. The colonial authorities' 'denial policy' removed boats and rice from coastal districts feared to lie in the path of a Japanese invasion, provincial trade barriers and hoarding pushed prices beyond the reach of the rural poor, famine was never officially declared, relief was slow, and the British War Cabinet limited food shipments to India. Most victims were landless labourers, fishermen and artisans in rural Bengal, hundreds of thousands of destitute people crowded into Calcutta, and many died of cholera, malaria and other diseases rather than outright starvation. Estimates of the death toll range from about 1.5 million, the figure of the official inquiry, to more than 3 million, and historians still debate the relative weight of crop failure, market and administrative failure, and decisions taken in London. The economist Amartya Sen, who witnessed the famine as a child, later used it to argue that famines are often caused by a collapse in people's ability to buy food rather than by a shortage of food alone.

title: Philadelphia Experiment (fringe claim)
summary: A popular legend claims the US Navy made the destroyer escort USS Eldridge invisible and teleported it from Philadelphia to Norfolk, Virginia.
description: The story originated in 1955–56 in letters sent to the UFO writer Morris K. Jessup by a man calling himself Carlos Miguel Allende (real name Carl Meredith Allen), who claimed to have watched the ship vanish in a greenish fog at the Philadelphia Navy Yard and reappear briefly at Norfolk, with crew members fused into the hull or driven insane. Allende linked the alleged experiment to Albert Einstein's work on a unified field theory. The tale was popularised by Charles Berlitz and William Moore's 1979 book and the 1984 film 'The Philadelphia Experiment', and it remains a staple of conspiracy literature about secret military technology.
mainstreamView: The US Navy's Office of Naval Research states that no such experiment took place, and Einstein never completed a unified field theory, let alone one that could be applied to ships. The Eldridge's surviving records and the accounts of men who served aboard it contradict the story, and Allende's own statements were inconsistent: at one point he admitted inventing it before retracting the admission. Historians suggest the legend grew out of genuine wartime research on degaussing, which made ships harder for magnetic mines to detect, 'invisible' only in that narrow sense.

title: D-Day: Allied landings in Normandy
summary: About 156,000 American, British, Canadian and other Allied troops land in Normandy by sea and air in the largest seaborne invasion in history.
description: Operation Overlord, commanded by General Dwight D. Eisenhower, opened with airborne drops overnight followed by landings on beaches codenamed Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, supported by nearly 7,000 vessels and some 11,000 aircraft. An elaborate deception plan, Operation Fortitude, had persuaded German commanders that the main attack would come at Calais. Allied casualties on the first day were at least 10,000, with the heaviest losses at Omaha Beach. The beachhead held, Paris was liberated in August, and the opening of this Western Front, together with Soviet advances in the east, sealed Germany's defeat.

title: Germany surrenders: Victory in Europe
summary: Germany's unconditional surrender takes effect, ending World War II in Europe a week after Hitler's suicide in besieged Berlin.
description: As Soviet forces stormed Berlin, Adolf Hitler killed himself on 30 April 1945, and his designated successor Karl Dönitz authorised surrender. General Alfred Jodl signed the unconditional surrender at Eisenhower's headquarters in Reims on 7 May, and a further signing took place at the Soviet headquarters in Berlin-Karlshorst late on 8 May, when it was already 9 May in Moscow, which is why Russia and several other countries mark victory on 9 May. The war in Europe had killed tens of millions and left the continent in ruins, divided into zones of occupation that foreshadowed the Cold War split between East and West.

title: United Nations founded
dateLabel: Charter signed 26 June 1945; in force 24 October 1945
summary: Fifty nations sign the United Nations Charter in San Francisco, creating a new organisation to maintain international peace and security.
description: Delegates from 50 countries drafted the charter at the San Francisco Conference, building on plans developed by the wartime Allies at Dumbarton Oaks and Yalta. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945 once the five permanent members of the Security Council (China, France, the Soviet Union, the United Kingdom and the United States) and a majority of other signatories had ratified it. Unlike the League of Nations it included all the major powers, though their veto in the Security Council often paralysed it during the Cold War. Its specialised agencies, peacekeeping missions and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 became central to postwar international cooperation, and its membership grew to 188 states by 1999 as decolonisation created new nations.

title: Atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
summary: US atomic bombs destroy Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing an estimated 150,000 to 246,000 people, mostly civilians, by the end of 1945.
description: Developed by the Manhattan Project and first tested at the Trinity site in New Mexico on 16 July 1945, the uranium bomb 'Little Boy' destroyed most of Hiroshima on 6 August, and the plutonium bomb 'Fat Man' devastated Nagasaki three days later. Blast, fire and radiation killed tens of thousands instantly and many more in the following months. Together with the Soviet declaration of war on Japan on 8 August, the bombings led Emperor Hirohito to announce Japan's surrender on 15 August. Whether they were necessary to end the war without an invasion remains debated by historians. They are the only use of nuclear weapons in war and opened the nuclear age.
